Best case, average case, and worst-case time complexities refer to the different running times that an algorithm can have, depending on the input.
 

 Best case time complexity is the best-possible running time for an algorithm, given a certain input. For example, if you have a search algorithm that performs a binary search through a sorted array, the best-case time complexity would be O(1), which means that the algorithm would find the desired element in the array in one operation.
 

 Average case time complexity is the average running time for an algorithm, calculated by considering all the possible inputs. For example, if you have a search algorithm that performs a linear search through an unsorted array, the average-case time complexity would be O(n/2), which is simplified to O(n) as the leading term n is dominating.
 

 Worst-case time complexity is the worst-possible running time for an algorithm, given a certain input. For example, if you have a search algorithm that performs a linear search through an unsorted array, the worst-case time complexity would be O(n) meaning that the algorithm would have to look through every element in the array to find the desired element.
 

 Best, average and worst-case time complexities are referred to using Big O notation, which is a mathematical notation used to describe the upper bound of an algorithm's running time, as a function of input size.
 

 Take for example a problem of finding an element in an unsorted array, possible solutions are Linear Search and Binary search.
 

 * Linear Search: in this case, the algorithm will look through each element of the array one by one till it finds the desired element. The best-case time complexity is O(1), if the desired element is the first element, the average-case time complexity is O(n/2) (simplified to O(n)) as the algorithm would have to search through half of the array to find the desired element on average. The worst-case time complexity is O(n), as the algorithm would have to search through every element in the array to find the desired element.
 * Binary Search: This is a searching algorithm that works on the principle of divide and conquer. Suppose we want to search for a target value in a sorted array, in this case, the algorithm will check the middle element first and then decide with which half of the array it should proceed. As a result, the number of operations will be log2(n), which is the number of bits required to represent the array size n using a binary number, best-case and average-case time complexity will be O(log n), whereas the worst case will be O(log n) as well, at the very worst the algorithm would have to search through every bit of the array, which still increases very slowly as the array size increases.
 

 As we can see from the examples, the best, average and worst-case time complexities can vary for different algorithms even when solving the same problem. It's essential to understand these concepts to have a good understanding of how well an algorithm will perform under different conditions.

1. Vertices: A graph consists of a set of vertices or nodes that are connected by edges.

2. Edges: An edge connects two vertices and represents a relationship between them. Edges can be undirected or directed.

3. Undirected vs. directed: An undirected edge connects two vertices in both directions, while a directed edge has a specific direction and connects only in one direction.

4. Weighted vs. unweighted: A weighted edge has a numerical value associated with it, such as the distance or cost between two vertices. An unweighted edge does not have a numerical value associated with it.

5. Connected vs. disconnected: A connected graph is a graph where any two vertices can be connected by a path of edges. A disconnected graph is a graph where there is at least one pair of vertices that cannot be connected by a path of edges.

6. Cycles: A cycle is a closed path in a graph where the first and last vertices are the same. A graph may contain cycles or be acyclic.

7. Degrees: The degree of a vertex is the number of edges that are connected to it. A vertex can have a degree of any positive integer, including zero.

8. Paths: A path in a graph is a sequence of edges that connect two vertices and do not repeat any vertices or edges.

9. Reachability: Reachability refers to whether one vertex can be reached from another vertex by following a path of edges.

10. Diameter: The diameter of a graph is the longest shortest path between any two vertices in the graph.

These are some of the basic properties of a graph data structure. Graphs are useful for representing relationships between objects and can be used in a variety of applications, such as routing and navigation, social networks, and machine learning.

Inline functions are a feature in C++ that allow the body of a function to be replaced with the function call site, essentially "inlining" the function's code where it is called. This is done at compile time, rather than waiting for the function to be called at runtime.
 

 The purpose of inline functions is to optimize performance by reducing the overhead of function calls. When a function is called, the program needs to transfer control to the function, save the state of the calling function, execute the function's code, and then return control back to the calling function. This involves a context switch and some memory overhead. By inlining the function's code, the compiler can eliminate these costs and improve the performance of the program.
 

 Inline functions can also improve cache utilization and reduce the number of virtual function calls in object-oriented programming, which can further optimize performance.
 

 It's important to note that the use of inline functions should be judicious, as overuse can lead to larger binary sizes and slower compile times. The compiler may also choose not to inline a function if it determines that the overhead of doing so outweighs the benefits. In such cases, the function will be called normally.
 

 In summary, inline functions are a performance optimization technique in C++ that can improve the efficiency of a program by reducing the overhead of function calls.

2. All external dependencies should be kept away from the core of the system, and should only be connected to it through clearly defined interfaces.

3. The system should be designed in layers, with each layer having dependencies only on the layers below it.

4. The layers should be designed to be as independent as possible, with minimal coupling between them.

5. The system should be designed to be open for extension, but closed for modification. This means that new functionality should be added by creating new code, not by modifying existing code.

6. The system should be designed to be resilient to change. This means that the system should be able to adapt to changes in requirements, technology, and other external factors without major changes to the core of the system.

Clean Architecture is a way of thinking about software design, and it can be applied to applications of any size or complexity. By following the principles of Clean Architecture, developers can create applications that are easier to maintain and test, and that are more adaptable to change over time.
